papers.title: Three-Dimensional Microtumor Formation of Infantile Hemangioma-Derived Endothelial Cells for Mechanistic Exploration and Drug Screening.
papers.abstract: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most prevalent type of vascular tumor in infants. The pathophysiology of IH is unknown. The tissue structure and physiology of two-dimensional cell cultures differ greatly from those in vivo, and spontaneous regression often occurs during tumor formation in nude mice and has severely limited research into the pathogenesis and development of IH. By decellularizing porcine aorta, we attempted to obtain vascular-specific extracellular matrix as the bioink for fabricating micropattern arrays of varying diameters via microcontact printing. We then constructed IH-derived CD31+ hemangioma endothelial cell three-dimensional microtumor models. The vascular-specific and decellularized extracellular matrix was suitable for the growth of infantile hemangioma-derived endothelial cells. The KEGG signaling pathway analysis revealed enrichment primarily in stem cell pluripotency, RAS, and PI3KAkt compared to the two-dimensional cell model according to RNA sequencing. Propranolol, the first-line medication for IH, was also used to test the model's applicability. We also found that metformin had some impact on the condition. The three-dimensional microtumor models of CD31+ hemangioma endothelial cells were more robust and efficient experimental models for IH mechanistic exploration and drug screening.

summary_en.motivation: To develop a physiologically relevant three-dimensional microtumor model for infantile hemangioma research.
summary_en.method: Decellularized porcine aorta was used as a vascular-specific bioink to fabricate micropattern arrays via microcontact printing.
summary_en.result: The 3D microtumor models exhibited enhanced stability and were suitable for mechanistic studies and drug screening.
summary_en.validation: RNA sequencing and testing with the clinical drug propranolol validated the model's applicability.

papers.title: High throughput 3D gel-based neural organotypic model for cellular assays using fluorescence biosensors.
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) organotypic models that capture native-like physiological features of tissues are being pursued as clinically predictive assays for therapeutics development. A range of these models are being developed to mimic brain morphology, physiology, and pathology of neurological diseases. Biofabrication of 3D gel-based cellular systems is emerging as a versatile technology to produce spatially and cell-type tailored, physiologically complex and native-like tissue models. Here we produce 3D fibrin gel-based functional neural co-culture models with human-iPSC differentiated dopaminergic or glutamatergic neurons and astrocytes. We further introduce genetically encoded fluorescence biosensors and optogenetics activation for real time functional measurements of intracellular calcium and levels of dopamine and glutamate neurotransmitters, in a high-throughput compatible plate format. We use pharmacological perturbations to demonstrate that the drug responses of 3D gel-based neural models are like those expected from in-vivo data, and in some cases, in contrast to those observed in the equivalent 2D neural models.

summary_zh.method: 利用人iPSC分化的神经元与星形胶质细胞共培养于纤维蛋白凝胶中，并引入荧光生物传感器

summary_en.motivation: To create a 3D neural organotypic model that recapitulates native tissue physiology for predictive drug assays
summary_en.method: Co-culture of human iPSC-derived dopaminergic/glutamatergic neurons and astrocytes in fibrin gels with genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors and optogenetics for real-time functional readouts
summary_en.result: The 3D model showed in-vivo-like drug responses, contrasting with 2D models in some cases
summary_en.validation: Pharmacological perturbation experiments with fluorescence biosensor readouts confirming model functionality
